page: Google Cloud Platform g2-standard-8 is a graphics-optimized virtual machine belonging to the g2 server family. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon processor with 8 dedicated vCPUs, 4 physical cores, and 2 threads per core running at a clock speed of 2.2 GHz. The CPU configuration includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 38 MB of L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 32.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. It integrates a single NVIDIA L4 GPU from the Ada Lovelace architecture family, which provides 22 GB of dedicated VRAM. This instance does not include any local storage and provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data reveals a clear performance contrast between CPU-bound tasks and GPU-accelerated workloads. The server demonstrates weak performance in single-core and multi-core CPU benchmarks, with Geekbench single-core and multi-core scores falling into the bottom 25%. Similarly, single-threaded gzip compression and bzip3 decompression are categorized as weak. However, the system achieves average tier performance in memory bandwidth tests, static web serving throughput at 6.69 GB/sec, and Redis SET operations at 6.2 million operations per second. In contrast, the integrated NVIDIA L4 GPU delivers top-tier performance in LLM inference benchmarks, processing 11784.81 tokens per second for a small 135M model and 2225.82 tokens per second for a medium 7B model.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the g2-standard-8 offers a specialized resource profile where the primary value resides in its GPU accelerator rather than raw CPU compute power. Because CPU performance is relatively weak, utilizing this instance for CPU-heavy compilation or general-purpose processing represents a suboptimal resource tradeoff. Instead, the hardware profile is optimized for workloads that offload computation to the GPU. Appropriate workloads include low-to-medium parameter LLM inference, machine learning model deployment, and graphics-accelerated tasks, while database operations and web serving remain viable secondary functions due to average memory and network throughput.
